You are reverse-engineering a C++ URL parser library **purely as a black box**.

The only artifact is the compiled binary: /workspace/dataset/test18_executable
There is NO library source available anywhere on disk (do not go looking for url_parser.h/.cpp — it does not exist). Do not try to disassemble or run 'strings'. Use ONLY behavioral probing: run the binary with argument values and observe stdout.

Usage: /workspace/dataset/test18_executable "<url>"
With fewer than 2 argv entries it returns exit code 1 and prints nothing.

It prints EXACTLY 18 lines, in this order (one per line, via std::cout << x << std::endl):
 1  scheme()          (string)
 2  authority()       (string)
 3  userinfo()        (string)
 4  host()            (string)
 5  port()            (int, prints -1 when absent)
 6  path()            (string)
 7  query()           (string)
 8  fragment()        (string)
 9  has_scheme()      (bool printed as 1/0)
10  has_authority()
11  has_userinfo()
12  has_host()
13  has_port()
14  has_path()
15  has_query()
16  has_fragment()
17  to_string()       (string)
18  is_valid()        (bool 1/0)

A labeled probe helper already exists at /tmp/probe.sh (takes any number of url args). If missing, recreate it:

  cat > /tmp/probe.sh << 'EOS'
  #!/bin/bash
  LABELS=(scheme authority userinfo host port path query fragment has_scheme has_authority has_userinfo has_host has_port has_path has_query has_fragment to_string is_valid)
  for arg in "$@"; do
    echo "=== INPUT: [$arg]"
    mapfile -t out < <(/workspace/dataset/test18_executable "$arg"; echo "EXIT:$?")
    for i in "${!LABELS[@]}"; do printf "  %-14s [%s]\n" "${LABELS[$i]}" "${out[$i]}"; done
  done
  EOS
  chmod +x /tmp/probe.sh

Note: /tmp/probe.sh renders empty fields as []. For inputs containing characters bash would mangle, invoke the binary directly with careful quoting, or use printf/hexdump to inspect raw bytes:
  /workspace/dataset/test18_executable "$URL" | od -c | head -40

ALREADY-ESTABLISHED FACTS (verified; you may re-verify but do not spend most of your budget here):
- A scheme is recognized ONLY when the literal "://" appears. "mailto:user@example.com" yields NO scheme and the entire input becomes path. "//example.com/path" yields no scheme and the whole thing is path (authority is parsed only when "://" was found).
- scheme() is LOWERCASED ("HTTP://EXAMPLE.COM" -> scheme "http"), but host() case is preserved ("EXAMPLE.COM").
- authority() is RECONSTRUCTED from userinfo/host/port, not the raw substring: "http://example.com:80abc" -> authority "example.com:80"; "http://example.com:" -> authority "example.com".
- port parsing behaves like std::stoi + a range check: "80abc"->80, "+80"->80, " 80"->80, "065"->65, "0"->0, but "-80"->absent, "65536"->absent, "2147483648"->absent, "abc"->absent, ""->absent. Absent port prints -1 with has_port 0 and is omitted from authority()/to_string().
- Splitting after authority: the FIRST '#' splits off fragment (so "#a#b" -> fragment "a#b"); then within the part BEFORE that '#', the FIRST '?' splits off query. "/p#a?b" -> fragment "a?b", no query.
- has_*() appear to be "field is non-empty" for strings ("http://example.com/#" -> fragment "" and has_fragment 0), and has_port() is port != -1. BUT has_authority() is NOT simply "authority string non-empty": "http://:8080" gives authority ":8080" yet has_authority 0 (host is empty there) — pin down the real rule.
- No path normalization ("/a/./b/../c" preserved), no percent-decoding ("%7E" preserved).
- is_valid(): "" -> 0, "http://" -> 0, "http://:8080" -> 0, but "example.com" -> 1, "/just/a/path" -> 1, "mailto:user@example.com" -> 1.

YOUR JOB: exhaustively probe your assigned family below. Run MANY probes (dozens — at least 40 distinct inputs; more is better). For every behavior you claim, you MUST have run the exact input. Derive precise, implementable rules (as if writing pseudocode), and explicitly flag anything ambiguous or surprising.

Return findings as structured output. Rules must be stated so a programmer can implement them without further probing. Include the concrete probe evidence (input -> the specific field values that matter) for each rule. Prefer many small precise rules over few vague ones.

YOUR ASSIGNED FAMILY:
HOSTILE / EXOTIC INPUTS — bytes, whitespace, size, and argv handling.
Probe: an input of only spaces; leading/trailing spaces around a full URL ("  http://h/p  "); embedded tab, newline (use $'\n' in bash), carriage return, NUL is impossible via argv so skip it; control chars; non-ASCII UTF-8 in every component (scheme, host, path, query, fragment) e.g. "http://exämple.com/pä?q=ä#ä" — confirm bytes pass through untouched (compare with 'od -c'); percent-encodings in every component including invalid ones ("%", "%zz", "%4"); characters like '\\', '|', '"', '<', '>', '^', '{', '}', '[', ']', backtick, '$'; a very long URL (e.g. host of 10000 chars, path of 100000 chars) — does it still work and is output correct; many colons/at-signs/hashes/question-marks; a URL that is just "://"; repeated "://".
ALSO verify the program's argv contract precisely: run with NO arguments (check exit code and that nothing is printed), with an empty-string argument, and with EXTRA arguments ("url1" "url2" — is only argv[1] used?). Confirm output is always exactly 18 lines terminated by newline, including for the empty input (use 'od -c' or 'wc -l' to be sure there is a trailing newline on the last line).

(2) query = everything after the FIRST '?' in `rest`; rest2 = prefix before it. (3) In rest2 only, search for the FIRST occurrence of the literal "://": if found at index i, scheme = rest2[0..i) (lowercased), and authority region starts at i+3; otherwise the whole rest2 is the path. Because '#'/'?' are removed first, a "://" that occurs after a '?' or '#' is NEVER treated as a scheme separator: "a?b://c" -> scheme "", path "a", query "b://c"; "#x://h" -> fragment "x://h", path "".

Authority region ends at the FIRST of '/', '?' or '#' — but since '?'/'#' were already stripped in steps 1-2, in practice it ends at the first '/' or at end of rest2. Everything from that '/' onward (inside rest2) is the path. "a://b://c" -> scheme a, host b, path "//c"; "http://h?q@x/p" -> authority "h", query "q@x/p".

Within the authority region: userinfo = text before the FIRST '@' (last '@' is NOT used): "http://a@b@c:80/p" -> userinfo "a", host "b@c", port 80. Then in the remainder, host = text before the FIRST ':' and port-token = text after it (later colons stay in the port token and are simply where stoi stops): "http://h:1:2/p" -> host "h", port 1. "http://u:p:q@h/p" -> userinfo "u:p:q", host "h".

NO IPv6 bracket support at all. "http://[::1]:8080/p" -> host "[", port -1 (stoi("::1]:8080") fails), authority "[", to_string "http://[/p" — i.e. the URL is silently corrupted and is_valid is still 1. Same for "http://[::1]/p".

NO trimming of any whitespace anywhere. Leading/trailing spaces are kept and become part of scheme and/or path: "  http://h/p  " -> scheme "  http" (has_scheme 1), path "/p  ", to_string "  http://h/p  ". An input of only spaces becomes the path (" " -> path " ", has_path 1, is_valid 1). Host may be pure whitespace: "http://   /p" -> host "   ", has_host 1.

Every byte other than the structural delimiters passes through completely untouched: tab, CR, LF, DEL(0x7f), control bytes 0x01-0x04, raw high bytes 0x80/0xFF, valid UTF-8 (U+00E4 = C3 A4), a UTF-8 BOM (EF BB BF), and invalid UTF-8. Verified byte-for-byte with od -c in scheme, host, path, query and fragment. No percent-decoding, no percent-validation, no encoding, no normalization: "%", "%zz", "%4", "%25" all survive verbatim in host/path/query/fragment, and '%' is even a legal scheme ("%://h" -> scheme "%", host "h").

scheme() lowercasing is ASCII-only, byte-wise (equivalent to tolower() in the C locale): 'A'-'Z' -> 'a'-'z'; bytes >= 0x80 are untouched. "htTPÜ://…" -> scheme "httpÜ" (C3 9C preserved); input "AAA\xC0\xDE://h/p" -> scheme "aaa\xC0\xDE". Non-alphabetic ASCII is unchanged. host()/path()/query()/fragment() case is never changed.

The scheme is an unconstrained byte string: it may contain spaces, tabs, '/', '%', high bytes, anything, as long as it appears before the first "://" and after the '?'/'#' stripping. "a/b://c" -> scheme "a/b", host "c"; "a b://c/d" -> scheme "a b"; " ://h/p" -> scheme " " (has_scheme 1) and to_string " ://h/p".

An input beginning with "://" yields an EMPTY scheme (has_scheme 0) but the authority IS still parsed: "://h/p" -> host "h", has_host 1, has_authority 1, path "/p". Special case: "://" alone produces output byte-identical to the empty input (all fields empty, port -1, all flags 0, to_string "", is_valid 0).

to_string() = (has_scheme() ? scheme + "://" + authority() : "") + path + (has_query() ? "?" + query : "") + (has_fragment() ? "#" + fragment : ""). Consequences: (a) when scheme is empty the authority is DROPPED from to_string even though has_authority may be 1 — "://h:80/p" -> to_string "/p" (lossy); (b) the authority part is emitted whenever has_scheme, regardless of has_authority — "http://u@:80/p" -> to_string "http://u@:80/p", "http://@/p" -> to_string "http:///p"; (c) empty query/fragment markers are dropped — "http://h/p?#" -> to_string "http://h/p".

authority() is rebuilt as (userinfo.empty()? "" : userinfo + "@") + host + (port==-1 ? "" : ":" + to_string(port)). An empty userinfo before '@' is dropped ("://@h" -> authority "h"); a non-numeric port token is dropped ("http://h:\"80\"/p" -> authority "h"); a truncated stoi result is re-serialized ("http://h:0x10/p" -> authority "h:0", "http://h:1:2/p" -> authority "h:1").

has_authority() == !host.empty() (i.e. it is exactly has_host()), NOT 'authority string non-empty'. Evidence: "://:80" -> authority ":80" but has_authority 0; "http://u@:80/p" -> authority "u@:80", has_userinfo 1, has_port 1, has_authority 0; "http://u@" -> authority "u@", has_authority 0. Across ~120 probes has_authority never differed from has_host.

has_scheme/has_userinfo/has_host/has_path/has_query/has_fragment are all exactly 'field string is non-empty' (a single space counts as non-empty: "http://h/p? # " -> query " " has_query 1, fragment " " has_fragment 1). has_port() == (port != -1), and port 0 counts as present ("http://:0" -> port 0, has_port 1).

is_valid() == (!host.empty() || !path.empty()), i.e. has_host() || has_path(). Nothing else matters — scheme, userinfo, port, query and fragment are all irrelevant. Evidence: "#f"->0, "?q"->0, "#?"->0, "a://"->0, "a://?q"->0, "a://#f"->0, "http://u@"->0, "http://u@?q"->0 (userinfo present), "http://:0"->0 (port present), ""->0, "://"->0; versus " "->1 (path " "), "@"->1 (path "@"), "http://h"->1 (host only), "http:///p"->1 (path only), "://h"->1.

Port token parsing is std::stoi + range check on the token after the first ':' in the host part: leading whitespace (space, tab, \v, \f, \r — all verified) and a leading '+' are skipped, digits are consumed greedily and parsing stops at the first non-digit, so "80abc"/"80 "/"0x10"/"1e3"/"8_0"/"8 0" -> 80/80/0/1/8/8; no leading digit after optional sign/space ("", "abc", '"80"', "::1]…") -> absent (-1); values > INT_MAX or negative ("-80", "65536", 100 nines) -> absent (-1). Absent port prints -1, has_port 0, and is omitted from authority() and to_string().

Repeated delimiters: only the first of each matters and the rest are literal data. "http://h/p??q?r" -> query "?q?r"; "http://h/p#a#b#c" -> fragment "a#b#c"; "http://h#f?q" -> fragment "f?q" and NO query; 1000 consecutive ':' after the host -> host "h", port -1; 1000 consecutive '@' -> userinfo "u", host = the remaining 999 '@' + "h" (length 1000).

Size: no internal length limit observed. A 120,016-byte URL (host 10,000 chars, path 100,000 chars, query 5,002, fragment 5,000, port 8080) parses with exact field contents and a byte-exact 120,016-char to_string round-trip. Inputs up to 131,070 bytes work; 131,072+ fails with execve 'Argument list too long' (rc 126 from the shell) — that is the Linux MAX_ARG_STRLEN limit (128 KiB per argument), not a program limit. No crash, no truncation, no quadratic slowdown noticed.
Option-looking arguments get no special treatment: "-h" -> path "-h", is_valid 1; "--help" -> path "--help". There is no flag parsing and no usage message on stdout for any argc >= 2.

Bare '@' or ':' or '//' with no "://" are plain path text: "@"->path "@"; ":"->path ":"; ":/"->path ":/"; "//"->path "//"; "://://"->scheme "" + path "//"; "http://://h" -> scheme http, authority empty, path "//h", to_string "http:////h".

This is consistent with ::tolower under the C locale, but a locale-sensitive build/environment (e.g. LC_ALL=de_DE.ISO-8859-1) could in principle map single-byte Latin-1 uppercase letters. I only tested the default environment locale, so 'ASCII-only' is certain for this environment but the mechanism (tolower vs explicit 'A'<=c<='Z') is not distinguishable behaviorally here.

to_string() is lossy/asymmetric in three ways that look like bugs rather than design: (a) when the scheme is empty but '://' was present, the authority is silently dropped ("://h:80/p" -> "/p"), so to_string is not a round-trip; (b) when has_scheme is true the authority is emitted even when has_authority() is false ("http://u@:80/p"); (c) '?' / '#' with empty content are dropped. IPv6 literals are simply broken ("http://[::1]:8080/p" -> host "["), and is_valid() still reports 1. There is no bracket handling whatsoever, so it is ambiguous whether a reimplementation is expected to reproduce this corruption — for byte-equality it must.

I did not manage to distinguish 'authority ends at first of /?#' from 'authority ends at first /' because '?' and '#' are already removed before the authority is parsed; both models predict every observed output. Implementing either is safe.
